rules.title: Prohibition on the Sale or Use of Coordinated Pricing Algorithms to Set Rents or Manage Occupancy Levels
rules.requirement: It is unlawful to sell, license, or provide to Berkeley landlords any coordinated pricing algorithm that sets or recommends rents or occupancy levels for Berkeley residential units. It is also unlawful for landlords to use such an algorithm when setting rents or occupancy levels. A coordinated pricing algorithm is one that uses nonpublic competitor data less than 90 days old.
rules.key_value: Sale and use banned; civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation (each month and each unit a separate violation)

coverage_conditions.text: Residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley. Covers vendors that sell, license, or provide coordinated pricing algorithms to Berkeley landlords, and landlords that use them. Competitor Data means nonpublic information less than 90 days old on rents, occupancy, and lease dates for properties not owned or managed by the landlord.

rules.exemptions: Excludes the following: (a) reports, studies, or presentations publishing aggregated, anonymous rental data that do not recommend rents, fees, occupancy, or lease terms; (b) products used to set rent or income limits under affordable housing guidelines; (c) market research for project financing, appraisals, or research, testing, or training for software development. Item (c) includes training models on Competitor Data only if that data is not used as an input when a recommendation is calculated.
rules.penalty: City Attorney may sue for damages, injunctive relief, restitution or return of illegal profits, and civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation. Aggrieved tenants may sue landlords who use the algorithms for injunctive relief, money damages, and civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation. Prevailing City Attorney or tenant is awarded attorney's fees and costs. Each month and each unit is a separate violation.
rules.citation: Berkeley Municipal Code Chapter 13.63 (§§ 13.63.030, 13.63.040), as amended by Ordinance No. 7,992-N.S.
rules.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a landlord to use a coordinated pricing algorithm described in subsection A when setting rents or occupancy levels for residential dwelling units in the City of Berkeley.
rules.extraction_note: The document shows the ordinance was passed to print at the November 18, 2025 Council meeting (first reading); it does not state the final adoption date or the effective date. The source URL references a December 2, 2025 agenda item, suggesting second reading and adoption then, but the text does not confirm it. Status of in_force is assumed given the query date. The ordinance amends an existing Chapter 13.63.

rules.title: Ronald V. Dellums Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance
rules.requirement: Berkeley landlords may not ask about or use criminal history or criminal background checks in rental advertising, applications, tenant selection or decisions. This includes refusing to rent, ending a tenancy, or charging a higher deposit or rent based on criminal history. Where an exception allows action based on criminal history, the landlord must give the applicant or tenant written notice and a chance to respond.
rules.key_value: Prohibits criminal-history inquiries and use in rental housing decisions

coverage_conditions.text: Rental housing providers in Berkeley, with regard to current or prospective tenants.

rules.exemptions: Lifetime sex offenders; limited exemptions for public housing and Section 8 properties; owner-occupied properties of 1-3 units where an owner of record lives in one unit as a primary residence; units under a rental agreement letting owners move back in per BMC 13.76.130 A.9; units occupied by existing tenants seeking to sublet or add or replace roommates.
rules.penalty: Administrative fines of at least $1,000 and up to $10,000 per violation. Civil damages, including actual damages or three times one month's rent. Punitive damages, attorneys' fees and costs, and injunctive relief.
rules.quoted_span: The Fair Chance Access to Housing Ordinance prohibits rental housing providers in Berkeley from asking about and using criminal history and/or criminal background checks in their rental housing advertising, applications, tenant selection process, or decision-making.
rules.extraction_note: This is the Rent Board summary page, not the ordinance text. The page states that City Council passed the ordinance on April 14, 2020; no effective date is given. rules.title: Annual General Adjustment capped at 5%

rules.title: Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy (criminal history screening)
rules.requirement: Covered housing providers may not use a blanket policy denying housing to anyone with arrests or convictions and must consider applicants case by case. rules.key_value: No blanket criminal-record bans; exclude non-conviction arrests, sealed/expunged convictions, juvenile records, and convictions older than 5 years

coverage_conditions.text: Housing providers receiving Department of Neighborhood Development (DND) funding and/or land, or that have income restricted units created under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy; also applied to the Office of Fair Housing and Equity Affirmative Marketing Program.

rules.exemptions: Does not apply where there is a direct relationship between a conviction and the housing sought, or an unreasonable risk of substantial harm to the safety of others; does not apply to current criminal behavior; yields where federal or state law imposes a conflicting criminal history requirement.
rules.interaction: The policy states that where federal or state law imposes a conflicting criminal history requirement, the federal or state law preempts this policy.
rules.citation: Boston Department of Neighborhood Development, Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy (February 2017)

rules.title: Cartwright Act: prohibition on use or distribution of common pricing algorithms (AB 325)
rules.requirement: It is unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, trust or conspiracy to restrain trade. It is also unlawful to use or distribute one while coercing another person to adopt a price or commercial term it recommends for the same or similar products or services in California.
rules.key_value: Ban on using or distributing a 'common pricing algorithm' (any methodology, including software, used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set or influence a price or commercial term) in restraint of trade or with coercion to adopt its recommendations.

coverage_conditions.text: Any person (as defined in Section 16702, excluding the end consumer of a product or service) who uses or distributes a common pricing algorithm, meaning any methodology, including a computer, software, or other technology, used by two or more persons, that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set, or otherwise influence a price or commercial term. Commercial term includes level of service, availability and output. Distribution includes selling, licensing, providing access to, or making available by any means, including by subscription.

rules.exemptions: Does not apply to the end consumer of a product or service, who is excluded from the definition of 'person'.
rules.penalty: Violation is a violation of the Cartwright Act, which the digest states is punishable as a crime. The section does not limit other antitrust remedies.
rules.interaction: Added to the Cartwright Act. Nothing in § 16729 impairs or limits the applicability of other antitrust laws. New § 16756.1 lowers the pleading standard for any Cartwright Act complaint: it suffices to allege facts making a contract, trust or conspiracy plausible, and the complaint need not allege facts excluding the possibility of independent action.
rules.quoted_span: It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.
rules.extraction_note: The statute is economy-wide and does not mention rental housing specifically. It is classified as algorithmic_rent_setting because it covers pricing software that uses competitor data to set prices, which would include rent. rules.title: Tenant Protection Act just cause eviction requirement (Civil Code 1946.2)
rules.requirement: After a tenant has lawfully occupied a unit for 12 months (or 24 months for one tenant if adult tenants were added), the owner may terminate only for a listed at-fault or no-fault just cause, which must be stated in the written notice. For no-fault terminations, the owner must pay relocation assistance or waive the final month's rent, equal to one month's rent, and curable violations require a notice to cure first.
rules.key_value: Just cause required after 12 months' occupancy; no-fault relocation assistance = one month's rent, paid within 15 calendar days of the notice

coverage_conditions.text: Residential real property, including dwellings or units in a mobilehome park, after the tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied it for 12 months (or, if adult tenants were added before 24 months, when all tenants have 12+ months or one tenant has 24+ months).

rules.exemptions: Transient/tourist hotel occupancy; nonprofit hospitals, religious facilities, extended care, licensed elderly residential care and adult residential facilities; school and higher-education dormitories; units where the tenant shares bathroom or kitchen with an owner who lives there; single-family owner-occupied residences renting no more than two units or bedrooms (including ADUs/JADUs) and mobilehomes; owner-occupied duplexes (neither unit an ADU/JADU) while the owner remains; housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years (unless a mobilehome); separately alienable units not owned by a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome park management, if the required exemption notice is given; deed- or agreement-restricted affordable housing; mobilehome homeowners. The section also does not apply where a qualifying local just cause ordinance applies.
rules.penalty: Noncompliance renders the termination notice void. An owner who attempts to recover possession in material violation is liable for actual damages, discretionary reasonable attorney's fees and costs, and up to three times actual damages plus possible punitive damages for willful, oppressive, fraudulent or malicious conduct. The Attorney General and city attorney or county counsel may seek injunctive relief.
rules.interaction: The state rule yields to a local just cause ordinance adopted on or before September 1, 2019, or to one adopted or amended after that date that is more protective and contains a binding finding saying so; in those cases the local ordinance applies. A property cannot be subject to both. Local ordinances adopted after September 1, 2019 that are less protective are unenforceable unless this section is repealed.
rules.citation: Cal. Civ. Code § 1946.2 (as amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 203 (AB 1529))
rules.quoted_span: Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.
rules.conflict_note: Subdivision (m) of the operative text states the section became operative on April 1, 2024. The history note says the current version, as amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 203 (AB 1529), is effective January 1, 2026. The operative-text date (2024-04-01) is used here.
rules.extraction_note: The section is repealed as of January 1, 2030 by its own terms. The signing or chaptering date of AB 1529 is not stated. The 15-year certificate-of-occupancy exemption is a rolling cutoff, not a fixed date, so no built cutoff was recorded. The rent cap in § 1947.12 is referenced only in the required notices and is not established by this document, so no rent_increase_limits record was created.

rules.title: California Tenant Protection Act statewide rent cap (Civil Code 1947.12)
rules.requirement: Over any 12-month period, an owner may not raise the gross rent for a covered unit by more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower. The cap is measured from the lowest gross rent in the prior 12 months, with no more than two increases in that period. Initial rent for a new tenancy may be set freely (vacancy decontrol).
rules.key_value: Lower of 5% + CPI or 10% per 12 months; max two increments

coverage_conditions.text: Residential real property, meaning any dwelling or unit intended for human habitation, including mobilehome park units. Applies to rent increases on or after March 15, 2019 (mobilehome tenancies: on or after February 18, 2021). Excludes housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years, unless it is a mobilehome.

rules.exemptions: Deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing; school and university dormitories; housing under stricter local rent control consistent with Costa-Hawkins (Ch. 2.7); housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years (except mobilehomes); separately alienable units such as single-family homes and condos not owned by a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member, or mobilehome park management, where the tenant received the required written exemption notice; owner-occupied duplexes where neither unit is an ADU or JADU; mobilehome homeowners as defined in Section 798.9.
rules.penalty: Civil action by the tenant for injunctive relief, damages equal to the excess rent, and discretionary attorney's fees and costs. Up to three times the excess for willful conduct or oppression, fraud or malice. The Attorney General and the city attorney or county counsel may enforce and seek injunctions. Three-year statute of limitations; waivers are void.
rules.interaction: This is the state rule. It does not apply to housing under a local rent or price control ordinance, consistent with Civil Code Chapter 2.7 (Costa-Hawkins), that limits annual increases to less than this cap. The section states it does not expand or limit local authority to regulate rents.
rules.citation: Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.12 (added by Stats. 2023, Ch. 290, Sec. 4 (SB 567))
rules.quoted_span: Subject to subdivision (b), an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower, of the lowest gross rental rate charged for that dwelling or unit at any time during the 12 months prior to the effective date of the increase.
rules.extraction_note: Operative text (subdivision (n)) sets the operative date as April 1, 2024. The history note says the law was effective January 1, 2024 and operative April 1, 2024. These describe the effective versus operative distinction rather than a conflict; the operative date is used here. The section is repealed as of January 1, 2030 (sunset), so it is in force on the query date. The 15-year certificate-of-occupancy exemption is a rolling cutoff with no fixed date, so built_cutoff fields are 'none'. The chaptered/signing date of SB 567 is not stated.

rules.title: Security deposit cap of one month's rent
rules.requirement: A landlord may not demand or receive security of more than one month's rent, in addition to first month's rent paid at or before move-in. The cap does not apply to security collected or demanded before July 1, 2024.
rules.key_value: 1 month's rent

coverage_conditions.text: Security for a rental agreement for residential property that is used as the dwelling of the tenant.

rules.exemptions: Advance payment of at least six months' rent for leases of six months or longer; agreed fees for tenant-requested alterations; small landlords (natural persons or LLCs of natural persons owning no more than two properties with no more than four units) may charge up to two months' rent; security collected or demanded before July 1, 2024.
rules.penalty: Bad-faith claim or retention of security may result in statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security, in addition to actual damages; actions may be brought in small claims court.
rules.quoted_span: (1) Except as provided in paragraph (2), (3), or (5), a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.
rules.extraction_note: Effective date taken from (c)(6), which says the subdivision does not apply to security collected or demanded before July 1, 2024. The section was most recently amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 340 (AB 414), effective January 1, 2026. No enactment date is stated.

rules.title: Small-landlord exception: up to two months' rent
rules.requirement: A landlord who is a natural person, or an LLC whose members are all natural persons, and who owns no more than two residential rental properties with no more than four units in total may charge security of up to two months' rent plus first month's rent. This exception does not apply when the prospective tenant is a service member.
rules.key_value: 2 months' rent

coverage_conditions.text: Landlords who are natural persons (including family trust settlors and beneficiaries) or LLCs of natural persons that own no more than two residential rental properties with no more than four dwelling units offered for rent.

rules.exemptions: Does not apply if the prospective tenant is a service member; a landlord may not refuse to rent to a service member because of this limit.
rules.penalty: Statutory damages of up to twice the security for bad-faith retention, in addition to actual damages.
rules.quoted_span: (A) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to two months’ rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy if the landlord meets both of the following requirements:
rules.extraction_note: The applicability date is inferred from (c)(6), which covers all of subdivision (c). The exception is not limited to owner-occupied properties.

rules.title: Service member higher-security disclosure and return
rules.requirement: If a landlord charges a service member a higher-than-standard security because of credit or housing history, the landlord must give a written explanation by lease signing. The extra amount must be returned after no more than six months if the tenant is not in arrears.
rules.key_value: Extra security returned within 6 months

coverage_conditions.text: Service members, as defined in Section 400 of the Military and Veterans Code, renting residential property they will reside in.

rules.penalty: Statutory damages of up to twice the security for bad-faith retention, in addition to actual damages.
rules.quoted_span: (4) On or after April 1, 2025, if a landlord or its agent charges a service member who rents residential property in which the service member will reside a higher than standard or advertised security pursuant to paragraph (1) due to the credit history, credit score, housing history, or other factor related to the tenant, the landlord shall provide the tenant with a written statement, on or before the date the lease is signed, of the amount of the higher security and an explanation why the higher security amount is being charged.

rules.title: 21-day itemized statement and deposit return
rules.requirement: Within 21 calendar days after the tenant vacates, the landlord must provide an itemized statement of deductions, with supporting documents and photographs, and return the remaining security. Deposits paid electronically must generally be returned electronically.
rules.key_value: 21 calendar days

coverage_conditions.text: Security for a rental agreement for residential property that is used as the dwelling of the tenant.

rules.exemptions: Supporting documentation is not required if deductions total $125 or less, or if the tenant signed a valid waiver; a tenant may still request documentation within 14 days.
rules.penalty: A landlord who fails to comply in bad faith forfeits any claim to the security; statutory damages of up to twice the security, in addition to actual damages.
rules.quoted_span: (m) The bad faith claim or retention by a landlord or the landlord’s successors in interest of the security or any portion thereof in violation of this section, or the bad faith demand of replacement of security in violation of subdivision (k), may subject the landlord or the landlord’s successors in interest to statutory damages of up to twice the amount of the security, in addition to actual damages.
rules.extraction_note: The quoted span is the penalty provision, because the 21-day sentence in (h)(1) is split across a layout line break. No specific effective date is stated for this subdivision; the section is amended effective January 1, 2026.

rules.title: Move-in and move-out photograph requirement
rules.requirement: The landlord must photograph the unit after the tenant returns possession, before and after any repairs or cleaning charged to the deposit. For tenancies beginning on or after July 1, 2025, the landlord must also photograph the unit at move-in.
rules.key_value: Photos required (move-out from 2025-04-01; move-in from 2025-07-01)

coverage_conditions.text: Residential tenancies with a security deposit; the move-in photo requirement applies to tenancies beginning on or after July 1, 2025.

rules.quoted_span: (2) Beginning April 1, 2025, the landlord shall take photographs of the unit within a reasonable time after the possession of the unit is returned to the landlord, but prior to any repairs or cleanings for which the landlord will make a deduction from or claim against the security deposit pursuant to this section, and shall also take photographs of the unit within a reasonable time after such repairs or cleanings are completed.
rules.extraction_note: The two parts of the rule start on different dates: move-out photos from April 1, 2025, and move-in photos for tenancies beginning on or after July 1, 2025.

rules.title: Prohibition on nonrefundable security
rules.requirement: A lease or rental agreement may not label any security as nonrefundable.
rules.key_value: No nonrefundable security

coverage_conditions.text: Security for a rental agreement for residential property that is used as the dwelling of the tenant.

rules.quoted_span: A lease or rental agreement shall not contain a provision characterizing any security as “nonrefundable.”
rules.extraction_note: No effective date is stated for this subdivision.

rules.title: Application screening fee cap, conditions, receipts and refunds
rules.requirement: Landlords may charge an application screening fee only up to actual out-of-pocket screening costs and never more than $30 per applicant (CPI-adjustable annually from January 1, 1998). They must not charge a fee when no unit is or will soon be available, and may charge only if they use a first-come qualified-applicant process or refund the full fee to unselected applicants. They must also give an itemized receipt, return unused amounts, and provide a copy of the credit report within seven days.
rules.key_value: $30 per applicant (CPI-adjusted annually since 1998-01-01); refund within 7 days of selection or 30 days of submission under option (B)

coverage_conditions.text: Applies when a landlord (an owner of residential rental property) or their agent receives a request to rent a residential property from an applicant, including guarantors and cosignors.

rules.exemptions: No refund is required for an applicant denied after consideration for not meeting the established screening criteria. An inadvertent fee from concurrent submissions is not a violation if refunded within seven days or applied to another unit at the applicant's option. Landlords may accept reusable screening reports under Section 1950.1. The section does not preempt federal or state housing assistance program rules on deposits and fees.
rules.interaction: Applies notwithstanding Section 1950.5. The screening fee is not 'security' under Section 1950.5 and is not an 'advance fee' under Bus. & Prof. Code § 10026.
rules.citation: Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6 (as amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 67, Sec. 29 (AB 1170))
rules.quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.
rules.extraction_note: The effective date of January 1, 2026 is that of the AB 1170 amendment shown in the history note. The signing date is not stated. The CPI-adjusted current cap amount is not given. No penalty is stated in this section.

rules.title: Prohibition on source-of-income discrimination in housing
rules.requirement: Owners of housing accommodations may not discriminate against or harass any person because of source of income, which includes federal, state, or local public assistance and housing subsidies such as Section 8 vouchers and HUD-VASH vouchers. Advertisements indicating a source-of-income preference or limitation are also unlawful.
rules.key_value: Source of income (including Section 8 and HUD-VASH vouchers) is a protected characteristic

coverage_conditions.text: Owners of any housing accommodation

rules.exemptions: Making a written or oral inquiry concerning the level or source of income is not source-of-income discrimination (subd. (p)(2)).
rules.quoted_span: For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information of that person.
rules.extraction_note: The effective date of 2024-01-01 is the effective date of the most recent amendment (Stats. 2023, Ch. 776, SB 267). The section's original effective date and the signing date are not stated. The document states no penalty.

rules.title: Income standard for subsidized applicants based on tenant's portion of rent
rules.requirement: When there is a government rent subsidy, a housing provider may not use a financial or income standard to assess rental eligibility unless the standard is based on the portion of the rent the tenant will pay.
rules.key_value: Income standard must be based on the tenant-paid portion of rent

coverage_conditions.text: Rental of housing in instances in which there is a government rent subsidy

rules.exemptions: Owners may still request information or documentation to verify employment, request landlord references, or verify identity (subd. (o)(2)).
rules.quoted_span: Use a financial or income standard in assessing eligibility for the rental of housing that is not based on the portion of the rent to be paid by the tenant.
rules.extraction_note: The effective date of 2024-01-01 is the effective date of the most recent amendment (SB 267, Stats. 2023, Ch. 776). The document does not say when this subdivision was first effective, and it states no penalty.

rules.title: Alternative to credit history for subsidized applicants
rules.requirement: When there is a government rent subsidy, a housing provider using credit history must offer the applicant the option of providing lawful, verifiable alternative evidence of ability to pay the tenant's portion of rent, such as benefit payments, pay records, or bank statements. If the applicant elects this option, the provider must give reasonable time to respond and must reasonably consider that evidence in lieu of credit history.
rules.key_value: Applicant may provide alternative evidence of ability to pay instead of credit history

coverage_conditions.text: Rental application process in instances in which there is a government rent subsidy

rules.exemptions: Owners may still request information or documentation to verify employment, request landlord references, or verify identity (subd. (o)(2)).
rules.quoted_span: Reasonably consider that alternative evidence in lieu of the person’s credit history in determining whether to offer the rental accommodation to the applicant.
rules.extraction_note: The effective date of 2024-01-01 is the effective date of the most recent amendment (SB 267, Stats. 2023, Ch. 776). The text does not separately date this clause, and it states no penalty.

rules.title: Cambridge Fair Housing Ordinance – source-of-income and protected-class discrimination in tenant selection
rules.requirement: Landlords and rental agents may not discriminate in renting, viewing, or setting the terms of tenancy based on protected categories, including source of income (Section 8 and public benefits). Any selection standard, such as ability to pay rent or to care for the apartment, must be applied equally and uniformly to all applicants.
rules.key_value: Source of income (including Section 8 and public benefits) is a protected category in rental housing

coverage_conditions.text: Real estate transactions in Cambridge, including viewing or renting an apartment and terms and conditions of tenancy.

rules.exemptions: Exemption for 2-family dwellings when the owner lives there.
rules.penalty: After a hearing, the Commission may file a criminal complaint in District Court, levy civil fines of up to $300 for each violation, seek injunctive relief in Superior Court, and seek damages, expenses and other relief; either party may remove a probable-cause case to Superior Court or the Attorney General's Office.
rules.quoted_span: Under the law, landlords, sellers and rental agents may use any reasonable standard to determine which applicants are selected, as long as that standard is applied equally and uniformly to all applicants.
rules.extraction_note: Source is an informational agency webpage summarizing the ordinance, not the ordinance text. Source of income is listed as a protected category under both the Human Rights Ordinance and the Fair Housing Ordinance. No enactment or effective dates are given for the ordinance; the Commission was established in 1984.

rules.title: Just Cause Ordinance (JCO) – just cause required and relocation assistance for no-fault evictions
rules.requirement: Landlords of covered rental units in the City of Los Angeles may terminate a tenancy only for listed at-fault or no-fault just causes. For no-fault evictions, such as owner or family move-in, demolition or removal from the market, they must pay relocation assistance.
rules.key_value: Just cause required; relocation assistance for no-fault evictions

coverage_conditions.text: Most residential properties in the City of Los Angeles not regulated by the RSO, including buildings newer than October 1, 1978 and single-family dwellings. The tenant must have lived in the unit at least six months or the original lease must have expired, whichever comes first.

rules.exemptions: Transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity or sorority houses, owner's roommate, cooperatives under certain circumstances, some non-profit homeless facilities or short-term substance abuse treatment centers, some HACLA or government-owned properties, and units subject to the RSO.
rules.interaction: The JCO covers units not regulated by the RSO. Single-family homes and condominiums exempt from state AB 1482 remain subject to the JCO.

rules.exemptions: Rent may reset to market rate after voluntary vacancy, certain at-fault evictions, City Attorney order evictions, or a Tenant Buyout Agreement. Condominium and townhome rent not regulated for tenancies commenced after December 31, 1995. Luxury exemption available on application.

rules.title: RSO legal reasons for eviction, notice, and relocation assistance
rules.requirement: RSO tenancies may be terminated only for listed at-fault causes (e.g., nonpayment, lease violation, nuisance, illegal use, refusal of access) or no-fault causes (owner/family move-in, resident manager, demolition/removal from market, government order, conversion to affordable housing). rules.key_value: Enumerated just causes; relocation assistance for no-fault evictions; 30/60-day notice (some 120 days or 1-year extension)

coverage_conditions.text: Rental units subject to the City's Rent Stabilization Ordinance (generally built on or before October 1, 1978); non-RSO properties are covered by the separate Just Cause Ordinance.

rules.title: RSO and SCEP fee pass-through surcharges
rules.requirement: Landlords may pass through the RSO fee ($1.61 per month) and the SCEP fee ($2.83 per month) to tenants, in addition to rent. They may do so only after registering the units and giving the tenant written notice.

rules.title: Relocation assistance and LAHD filing for no-fault evictions under the RSO and JCO
rules.requirement: Before evicting for a no-fault reason from an RSO or JCO unit, a landlord must file a Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD. Only then may the landlord serve the termination notice, and a copy must be filed with LAHD within 3 days. The landlord must pay relocation assistance per unit within 15 days of serving the notice, either directly or through an escrow account.
rules.key_value: Jul 1, 2026–Jun 30, 2027 amounts: Eligible $11,000 (<3 yrs) / $14,400 (3+ yrs or low income); Qualified $23,150 / $27,400; Mom & Pop owner/family move-in $10,550 eligible / $21,250 qualified; JCO single-family dwelling owned by natural person: one month's rent. Payment due within 15 days of notice.

coverage_conditions.text: Units covered by the Rent Stabilization Ordinance (RSO) or the Just Cause Ordinance (JCO). Demolition and conversions under LAMC 47.06 and 47.07 are covered whether or not the property is subject to the RSO or JCO.

rules.exemptions: No relocation is owed when replacing a resident manager with another resident manager, unless the manager-tenant receives free or reduced rent and no other compensation. No relocation is owed for an eviction required by hazardous conditions from a natural disaster not caused by landlord negligence. A landlord may offset accumulated unpaid rent, except where the termination is required by a government order to vacate or an order for an unpermitted dwelling. rules.title: Statewide prohibition on local rent control, with limited voluntary exception (G.L. c. 40P, § 4)
rules.requirement: Massachusetts cities and towns may not enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind. The only exception is for a municipality that accepts chapter 40P, and its regulation must be voluntary for owners after six months, may not regulate evictions or similar matters, may not cover owners of fewer than ten units or units with fair market rent above $400, and must compensate owners from general funds.
rules.key_value: Local rent control prohibited; exception limited to voluntary programs that exclude owners of fewer than 10 units and units with fair market rent above $400, with municipal compensation to owners

coverage_conditions.text: Applies statewide to all cities and towns. Any permitted local rent control may not apply to any rental unit owned by a person or entity owning less than ten rental units, or to any unit with a fair market rent exceeding $400. Owner compliance must be voluntary after six months from initial adoption.

rules.exemptions: Any permitted local regulation may not cover units owned by a person or entity owning fewer than ten rental units, or units with fair market rent over $400. It may not regulate occupancy, services, evictions, condominium conversion or removal of properties from regulation.
rules.interaction: This is a state rule that preempts local rent control in Massachusetts. Any local rent control is allowed only within the narrow conditions of § 4 for municipalities that accept chapter 40P.

rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act – ban on criminal-history inquiries before a conditional offer
rules.requirement: Housing providers may not ask about an applicant's criminal record, orally, in writing or on an application, until after making a conditional offer. The only exceptions are methamphetamine production on federally assisted housing premises and lifetime sex-offender registration. Before accepting any application fee, the provider must disclose in writing whether criminal history is reviewed and that the applicant may submit evidence of inaccuracies, rehabilitation or other mitigating factors.
rules.key_value: No criminal-record inquiry before conditional offer

coverage_conditions.text: Rental dwelling units offered for rent by a housing provider for residential purposes, other than a dwelling unit in an owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units.

rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units. Providers may consider methamphetamine manufacture or production on federally assisted housing premises and lifetime sex-offender registration before the offer.
rules.penalty: Penalties are imposed by the Division on Civil Rights: up to $1,000 for a first violation, up to $5,000 if there is one other violation within five years, and up to $10,000 if there are two or more other violations within seven years. The director may also order cease and desist, remedial housing offers and return of the application fee, and may direct up to $1,000 of the penalty to the applicant. No private court action is allowed.
rules.quoted_span: A housing provider shall not make any oral or written inquiry regarding an applicant’s criminal record prior to making a conditional offer.
rules.extraction_note: The effective date is calculated from §14: the act takes effect on the first day of the seventh month next following enactment, and it was approved June 18, 2021. The document does not state 2022-01-01 explicitly.

rules.title: Fair Chance in Housing Act – post-offer criminal record limits, lookback periods and withdrawal procedure
rules.requirement: Housing providers may never consider arrests or charges without conviction, or expunged, pardoned, vacated, juvenile or sealed records. After a conditional offer, they may consider only listed serious crimes and recent indictable convictions: 6 years for first degree, 4 years for second or third degree, and 1 year for fourth degree. An offer may be withdrawn only after an individualized assessment shows, by preponderance of the evidence, that withdrawal is necessary for a substantial, legitimate, nondiscriminatory interest, and the provider must give written reasons and an opportunity to appeal.
rules.key_value: Lookback 6 yrs (1st degree) / 4 yrs (2nd-3rd degree) / 1 yr (4th degree)

coverage_conditions.text: Rental dwelling units offered for rent by a housing provider for residential purposes, other than a dwelling unit in an owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units.

rules.exemptions: Owner-occupied premises of not more than four dwelling units. Convictions for murder, aggravated sexual assault, kidnapping, arson, human trafficking, specified sexual offenses, or crimes requiring lifetime sex-offender registration may be considered without a lookback limit.
rules.penalty: Penalties are imposed by the Division on Civil Rights: up to $1,000 for a first violation, up to $5,000 if there is one other violation within five years, and up to $10,000 if there are two or more other violations within seven years. The director may also order cease and desist, remedial housing offers and return of the application fee, and may direct up to $1,000 of the penalty to the applicant.
rules.quoted_span: A housing provider may withdraw a conditional offer based on an applicant's criminal record only if the housing provider determines, by preponderance of the evidence, that the withdrawal is necessary to fulfill a substantial, legitimate, and nondiscriminatory interest.
rules.extraction_note: The effective date is calculated from §14 (first day of the seventh month after the June 18, 2021 approval) and is not stated explicitly. Applicants may request, within 30 days of withdrawal, the information the provider relied on, which must be provided free of charge within 10 days.

rules.title: Residential rental property application fee not to exceed $50
rules.requirement: A landlord or its agent may not charge an application or similar fee above $50 to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental unit. The cap is adjusted each January 1 by the CPI change, and only if that change is positive.
rules.key_value: $50 maximum application fee, CPI-adjusted annually starting January 1 of the year after enactment

coverage_conditions.text: Fees to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes; does not apply to dwelling units in one-family or two-family dwellings offered for rent.

rules.exemptions: (1) A dwelling unit in a one-family or two-family dwelling offered for rent. (2) A licensee of the New Jersey Real Estate Commission, unless the licensee is the landlord of the property.
rules.penalty: Penalty of up to $500 for a first offense, up to $750 for a second offense, and up to $1,000 for each later offense. Penalties are enforced by summary proceedings under the Penalty Enforcement Law of 1999 on complaint of the Director of Consumer Affairs or the Attorney General. The amount wrongfully charged is taken from the collected penalty and remitted to the applicant.
rules.quoted_span: A landlord, or agent thereof, shall not require an application or other similar fee to apply to lease or sublease a residential rental property for dwelling purposes, which exceeds $50.

The one- and two-family exemption applies regardless of owner occupancy, so exempts_small_owner_occupied is false; min_units of 3 is derived from that exemption. The CPI adjustment uses CPI-U New York-Northern New Jersey-Long Island, with the 12-month period ending October 31; the State Treasurer determines the adjustment by December 1, and the Director of Consumer Affairs publishes the limit annually. The quoted_span keeps the source document's line breaks.

rules.title: Security deposit cap of 1.5 months' rent (Security Deposit Law)
rules.requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit greater than one and one-half times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. Prepaid rent, including last month's rent, counts toward the cap, so no more than 2.5 months' rent may be required at lease inception.

rules.title: Anti-Eviction Act good cause requirement
rules.requirement: A residential landlord may not evict a tenant or refuse to renew a written or oral lease without one of the statutory good causes, such as nonpayment, disorderly conduct, damage, rule or lease violations, or an unpaid lawful rent increase. A Notice to Quit, and for some causes a Notice to Cease, is required, with notice periods from three days to three years depending on the cause.
rules.key_value: Good cause required for eviction and non-renewal

coverage_conditions.text: The Anti-Eviction Act applies to most residential rental properties including single-family homes, mobile homes and land in a mobile home park, apartment buildings, and complexes, and rooming and boarding homes.

rules.exemptions: May not apply to two- or three-unit owner-occupied premises with two or fewer rental units; hotel, motel or guest house transient or seasonal guests (unless the occupant has no alternate residence and lives there continually); units held in trust for a developmentally disabled immediate family member who permanently occupies the unit.
rules.penalty: Landlord who evicts for owner occupancy and does not occupy the unit for 6 months, or who returns a board-up, demolition or retirement property to residential use within 5 years, is liable for three times damages plus attorney fees and costs; civil penalty up to $10,000 per violation for the retirement/removal case (N.J.S.A. 2A:18-61.6).
rules.quoted_span: No residential landlord may evict or fail to renew a lease, whether it is a written or an oral lease without good cause.

rules.title: Relocation assistance for illegal-occupancy evictions

If the landlord does not pay at least five days before removal, the tenant may be paid from a municipal revolving fund, which the landlord must repay.

rules.title: Rent increases must not be unconscionable
rules.requirement: New Jersey has no statewide rent control, but a rent increase must not be unconscionable and must comply with any municipal rent control ordinance. The landlord must terminate the existing lease with proper notice and offer a new lease at the higher rent; the rent cannot be raised mid-lease.

coverage_conditions.text: Residential tenancies covered by the Anti-Eviction Act; municipalities may separately adopt rent control or rent leveling ordinances.

rules.interaction: Municipal rent control ordinances, where adopted, also govern rent increases. A tenant may complain to the municipal rent control board where one exists; otherwise a court decides unconscionability in an eviction action.
rules.quoted_span: The increase in rent must not be unconscionable; it must not be so unreasonable as to shock the conscience of a fair and honest person and must comply with any municipal ordinances governing rent increases.
rules.extraction_note: Unconscionability factors (per case law): size of increase, landlord's expenses and profitability, comparable rents, bargaining position, and the judge's general knowledge. A tenant may withhold the disputed increase but risks an eviction suit.

rules.title: No rent increases to cover conversion costs
rules.requirement: When a building is converted to condominium, cooperative or fee simple ownership, rents may not be raised to cover costs resulting solely from the conversion. Increases for new services or amenities are still allowed.

coverage_conditions.text: All landlord-tenant relationships, with listed exceptions.

rules.exemptions: Two-family owner-occupied dwellings; rooms in an owner- or resident-occupied single home; single-sex residences (e.g., YMCA) and age-restricted housing as to familial status (N.J.S.A. 10:5-5(n)).
rules.penalty: Monetary damages, an order to rent the unit to the complainant, and fines and penalties up to $10,000 for a first offense (N.J.S.A. 10:5-14.1a(a)).
rules.quoted_span: The New Jersey Law Against Discrimination (LAD), N.J.S.A. 10:5-12(g) to -(h), prohibits discrimination when selling or renting property and requires equal treatment in the sale or rental of housing regardless of race, creed, color, national origin, ancestry, sex, marital status, civil union status, domestic partnership status, familial status, affectional or sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, mental and physical disability, nationality, or source of lawful income.

rules.title: NJ Law Against Discrimination: source of lawful income protection in housing
rules.requirement: Landlords may not discriminate in housing based on the source of lawful income or the source of lawful rent payment a tenant uses. For example, a landlord cannot deny a Section 8 HUD voucher holder an apartment based solely on that source of income.
rules.key_value: Source-of-income discrimination prohibited (incl. Section 8 vouchers)

coverage_conditions.text: Applies to the sale or rental of all property including open land, whether for business or residential purposes, with listed exceptions.

rules.exemptions: Rental of a single apartment or flat in a two-family dwelling whose other unit is occupied by the owner as a residence; rental of a room or rooms by the owner or occupant of a one-family dwelling occupied as their residence; religious organizations giving preference to persons of the same religion; familial-status prohibition does not apply to housing for older persons (N.J.S.A. 10:5-5mm).
rules.quoted_span: The LAD also prohibits housing discrimination based on the source of lawful income or source of lawful rent or mortgage payment a tenant or purchaser uses.
rules.extraction_note: Source is a Division on Civil Rights informational brochure (rev. 06.18.15), not statutory text; no specific section cite, effective or enactment date given. Enforcement: complaint may be filed with the Division within 180 days of the alleged violation or in NJ Superior Court within two years; no specific monetary penalties stated. Brochure does not address criminal-history screening.

rules.title: Forbidding the Algorithmic Inflation of Rent (FAIR) Act
rules.requirement: Rental property owners may not pay for or use the services of a coordinator (algorithmic revenue management software or an algorithmic device that performs a coordinating function). No person may perform a coordinating function or engage in or facilitate parallel pricing coordination on rental prices, material lease terms, or occupancy levels.
rules.key_value: Ban on using coordinator / algorithmic rent-setting services; violation of NJ Antitrust Act

coverage_conditions.text: Rental property owners owning one or more residential dwelling units (any house, apartment, accessory unit, or other unit intended to be used as a primary residence in the State); coordinators operating algorithmic revenue management software or algorithmic devices performing a coordinating function.

rules.exemptions: Residential dwelling unit excludes inpatient medical care, licensed long-term care, and detention or correctional facilities. Algorithmic device excludes non-AI spreadsheets requiring human analysis and databases that only query unprocessed data. Coordinating function excludes research/statistical analysis not used to set or recommend terms, free public rent estimates, real estate brokerage databases available on equal terms that do not set/recommend prices or collect competitively sensitive information, and government affordability controls. Coordinator excludes government entities setting rents through affordability controls.
rules.penalty: Conduct is unlawful and a violation of the New Jersey Antitrust Act (C.56:9-1 et seq.); sections 6 through 17 of P.L.1970, c.73 (C.56:9-6 through 9-17) apply to violations. Attorney General to maintain a complaint portal.
rules.interaction: State law supplementing the New Jersey Antitrust Act; municipalities are prohibited from enacting ordinances that conflict with this act, except ordinances explicitly authorized or required by other law.
rules.quoted_span: a rental property owner, or any agent, representative, or subcontractor thereof, to receive, subscribe to, contract for, or otherwise exchange any form of consideration in return for the use of, the services of a coordinator;

rules.title: Residential Tenant Protections – just cause required for termination of tenancy
rules.requirement: A landlord may not terminate a tenancy (occupancy over 30 days) without at-fault just cause (12 listed grounds, such as nonpayment, material lease breach, nuisance or criminal activity) or good-faith no-fault just cause (owner or relative move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, a government order, or demolition or substantial remodel). Curable violations require a written notice to cure first, and no-fault notices must meet content requirements and give 30 or 60 days' notice under Civil Code 1946.1.
rules.key_value: Just cause required; at-fault and no-fault causes enumerated

coverage_conditions.text: Residential rental property, meaning any dwelling or unit intended for human habitation, including mobilehome park units. A tenancy is a right to occupy for more than 30 days and excludes fixed-term leases of three months or less. Many property types are exempt under §98.0703.

rules.exemptions: Transient and tourist hotels; short-term residential occupancy; deed- or agreement-restricted affordable housing; subsidized affordable housing (but not Section 8); mobilehomes under the Mobilehome Residency Law; nonprofit hospitals, religious, care and adult residential facilities and nonprofit transitional housing; school dormitories; units sharing a bathroom or kitchen with a resident landlord; owner-occupied single-family residences (renting up to two bedrooms, ADUs or JADUs); owner-occupied two-unit structures; housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (except mobilehomes); separately alienable units whose landlord is not a REIT, corporation, LLC with a corporate member or mobilehome park management, if the required written exemption notice is given.
rules.penalty: Tenant may sue for injunctive and equitable relief and money damages, including punitive damages, and may raise violations as an affirmative defense. Wrongful eviction damages are not less than three times actual economic damages, and attorney's fees and costs may be awarded at the court's discretion. Noncompliant termination notices are void, and the City may enforce with civil and criminal remedies.
rules.interaction: The Division requires just cause consistent with California Civil Code section 1946.2 and states that its rights are in addition to any existing rights under state or federal law. It does not state that it replaces the state rule.
rules.citation: San Diego Municipal Code §§98.0704, 98.0706 (O-21647 N.S.; amended O-21769 N.S.)
rules.quoted_span: A landlord shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause.
rules.extraction_note: Added 5-25-2023 by O-21647 N.S., effective 6-24-2023; amended 2-27-2024 by O-21769 N.S., effective 3-28-2024. The new-construction exemption is a rolling 15-year certificate-of-occupancy window rather than a fixed date, so no built cutoff was recorded. Owner move-in requires the intended occupant to move in within 90 days and occupy for 12 continuous months. Leases entered on or after 6-24-2023 must allow owner move-in or the tenant must agree in writing.

rules.title: Relocation assistance and right to re-rent for no-fault just cause terminations
rules.requirement: For no-fault terminations, the landlord must provide relocation assistance equal to two months' actual rent (three months for senior or disabled tenants), either as a direct payment within 15 days of notice or as a rent waiver, regardless of the tenant's income or length of tenancy. If the unit is re-offered for rent within five years after an owner move-in, government-order or demolition/remodel eviction, the landlord must first offer it to the displaced tenant who asked in writing.
rules.key_value: 2 months' rent; 3 months for seniors (62+) or disabled tenants

coverage_conditions.text: Tenancies in residential rental property subject to Division 7 that are terminated for no-fault just cause.

rules.exemptions: Properties exempt under §98.0703. A tenant found at fault for conditions triggering a government order to vacate is not entitled to relocation assistance.
rules.penalty: A landlord who fails to provide required relocation assistance is liable for not less than three times the required relocation assistance plus actual economic damages. Failure to strictly comply with §98.0706 voids the termination notice.
rules.interaction: Relocation assistance is credited against any other federal, state or local relocation assistance and is in addition to the return of any deposit. The Division supplements Civil Code section 1946.2.
rules.quoted_span: If the tenant is a senior or disabled, the direct payment to the tenant shall be in an amount equal to three months of actual rent under the tenant’s lease in effect at the date of the notice.
rules.extraction_note: Buyout agreements must exceed this relocation amount or are void (§98.0707(d)). Landlords must also notify the Housing Commission within three business days once the Commission's portal exists.

rules.title: Prohibition of Anti-Competitive Automated Rent Price-Fixing Ordinance (proposed)
rules.requirement: Would make it unlawful for any person to sell, license or otherwise provide an algorithmic device to a landlord, and unlawful for a landlord to use one to set rental rates or occupancy levels. An algorithmic device is software that uses nonpublic competitor data to advise or recommend rents or occupancy levels; reports based on public data or on aggregated data more than 90 days old, and affordable-housing program tools, are excluded.
rules.key_value: Ban on sale, licensing and use of algorithmic rent-setting devices; civil penalties up to $1,000 per violation

coverage_conditions.text: Residential rental property in the City of San Diego; applies to any person selling, licensing or providing an algorithmic device to a landlord and to landlords using one.

rules.exemptions: Software or products that publish reports on rental rates or occupancy levels from aggregated historical nonpublic competitor data more than 90 days old, or from information available to the general public, and that do not recommend rates or occupancy levels for future leases or renewals. Software or products used to set rental rates or income limits under local, state or federal affordable housing program guidelines.
rules.penalty: A tenant may sue a landlord for injunctive relief, damages, or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation. A prevailing tenant recovers costs and reasonable attorney's fees, and lease clauses limiting fee recovery are unenforceable. Each month of use, and each property where a device is used, is a separate violation. Remedies are cumulative.
rules.citation: Proposed San Diego Municipal Code ch. 9, art. 8, div. 11, §§98.1101-98.1104 (O-2025-107)
rules.quoted_span: It is unlawful for a landlord to use an algorithmic device to set rental rates or occupancy levels for residential rental property.

rules.title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance just cause eviction requirement
rules.requirement: A landlord may evict a tenant from a unit covered by the Rent Ordinance only for one of 17 listed just cause reasons, and that reason must be the dominant motive for the eviction. Expiration of the lease or a change in ownership is not just cause, and removing housing services such as parking, storage or laundry also requires just cause.
rules.key_value: 17 just cause reasons; reason must be dominant motive

coverage_conditions.text: Rental units covered by the Rent Ordinance. This includes tenancies exempt from the rent increase limits, such as newly constructed units that first obtained a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979, tenancies eligible for a rent increase under the Costa-Hawkins Rental Housing Act, and some tenancies where rent is regulated by another government agency.

rules.penalty: A landlord who evicts or tries to evict a tenant unlawfully may be subject to substantial civil and/or criminal liability.
rules.quoted_span: In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction. Note that the mere expiration of a rental agreement or a change in ownership does not constitute "just cause" for eviction.
rules.extraction_note: This is an official Rent Board summary page, not the ordinance text. No effective or enactment date is stated. The June 13, 1979 Certificate of Occupancy date limits only rent increase coverage; post-1979 units remain subject to just cause, so no construction cutoff is recorded for this rule. Notice and relocation requirements are not described. Permitted causes include nonpayment, breach, nuisance, illegal use, refusal to renew, denial of access, unapproved subtenant, owner or relative move-in, condo conversion, demolition, capital improvements, substantial rehabilitation, Ellis Act withdrawal, lead remediation, development agreement, expired Good Samaritan tenancy, and Planning Code Section 317 development.
